correctness.rationale: Reconstructed the inverse-Rayleigh CDF by integrating its density and independently conditioned on Beta(q,1). Exact survival is 1-e^{-a}+a^{q/2}Gamma(1-q/2,a), valid for a>0,q>0. Writing eta=(q-2)/2=w/log(1/a), the split integral on (a,1) is exactly L Phi(w). The remaining kernel is differentiable at eta=0 with value -EulerGamma, and truncation after multiplication by a^eta contributes O(a), uniformly on |w|<=K. This proves the two-term O(1/L) bracket. For the independent triangular array, L=log n+log log n+2log x and eta=kappa/log n; Taylor expansion provides the explicit O((log log n)^2/(log n)^2) second-order nS, and (1-S)^n converges to exp(-Phi(kappa)/x^2), with nS^2=O(1/n). The actual standalone Python checker passed 14 independent conditional-integral identities and the prescribed asymptotic cross-checks. Finite checks support but do not replace the proof.

originality.rationale: The fixed-shape regular-variation and power/log regimes for the same SIR law are already covered and explicitly excluded from novelty. In contrast, a uniform two-term expansion when the beta shape itself moves as 2+2w/log(z^2/theta), including the Euler constant term, implies a nontrivial triangular-array Fréchet crossover and an explicit (log log n)/log n correction. Pointwise regular variation at every fixed shape has no uniformity in a moving shape. The 2026 full source contains the CDF and an unevaluated fixed-shape regular variation ratio, but no triangular-array maximum analysis. The inspected general 2007 product-tail theory concerns fixed product distributions, and the 2023 inverse-Weibull construction uses a bounded multiplier. No covering mathematical implication was identified in the searches; unindexed priority remains possible.
residual_risks: A general theorem in uncatalogued or unindexed moving-index product-tail literature could subsume the specific uniform crossover.

value.rationale: Two distinct regularly varying tail powers compete at the natural parameter q=2. For extreme quantiles and sample maxima, calibrations that hold q fixed cannot resolve a q_n=2+O(1/log n) regime. The nonconstant Phi(kappa) crossover gives the correctly normalized Fréchet limit and an explicit (log log n)/log n finite-size drift, revealing slow convergence that affects practical extreme-event calibration. It is a motivated complete critical-window result and not a mere restatement of the previously known fixed-q tail-index classification. No distribution-free or finite-n risk guarantee is claimed.
